seed.description: Integer currently only used for selecting starting position.

strictMode.description: If true, agents must return only {'submission': int} (no extra fields like 'thoughts'), and per-agent TIMEOUT/ERROR/INVALID counts as a loss for the offending agent only — other agents win. If false (default), any agent error halts and voids the entire episode, matching the lenient research-mode behavior.

useImage.description: If true, indicates the observation is intended to be rendered as an image. Note that currently the agent harness is responsible for the actual rendering; no image is passed in the observation.

useOpenings.description: Whether to start from a position in an opening book.

currentPlayer.description: ID of player whose turn it is.

legalActionStrings.description: List of OpenSpiel legal action strings. Only included if includeLegalActions is true.

legalActions.description: List of OpenSpiel legal action integers. Only included if includeLegalActions is true.

openSpielGameName.description: Short name of the OpenSpiel game.

playerId.description: ID of the agent receiving this observation.

serializedGameAndState.description: Enables reconstructing the Game and State objects.

remainingOverageTime.description: Total remaining banked time (seconds) that can be used in excess of per-step actTimeouts -- agent is disqualified with TIMEOUT status when this drops below 0.

action.thoughts:
The current board has a single x in column 3, row 5 (bottom) and an o directly above it in column 3, row 4. This is an early-game position where developing connections and controlling central bottom rows is key. All columns are legal (none have row 0 occupied).

Playing in column 3 (row 3) stacks an x above the o but creates no connections (x-o-x vertically, separated) and allows the opponent to claim a valuable adjacent bottom spot (e.g., column 2 or 4 row 5). This is suboptimal.

Instead, playing in column 2 (or symmetrically column 4) drops an x into row 5, creating an immediate horizontal two-in-a-row (columns 2-3, row 5: x-x). This sets up a classic double-threat fork:
- Opponent cannot block both extensions (column 1 and column 4) in one move.
- If opponent stacks column 3 (row 3 o), you extend to three horizontally (e.g., column 4 row 5 x).
- If opponent blocks one side (e.g., column 4 row 5 o), you extend the other (column 1 row 5 x), creating a three-in-a-row threat that forces their next response.
- This controls central bottom space, enhances diagonal/horizontal potentials, and outpaces vertical stacking risks (opponent's single o is far from a threat; blockable later if needed).

Columns 2 and 4 are equivalent by symmetry (empty board left/right of column 3). Column 2 is selected as the tiebreaker (lowest index).

Final Answer: 2

action.thoughts:
The current board position is very early in the game, with only three pieces placed total (one 'o' and two 'x's). No player has an immediate threat of three-in-a-row that would force a block on the next turn, and no one can win on this move since a single placement can at most create a pair of 'o's.

Standard Connect Four strategy prioritizes controlling the center column (column 3) early to maximize future options for vertical, horizontal, and both diagonal directions. Placing here drops the piece to row 3 in column 3 (above the existing 'o' at row 4), creating a vertical pair of 'o's in the center. This also occupies the key central column, limiting 'x's ability to build through it while setting up multiple expansion paths (e.g., extending upward or diagonally outward).

Alternative placements (such as column 2 to create a horizontal pair at row 4, or column 4 to start a diagonal) are playable but less flexible for long-term control compared to the center. Column 3 is therefore the optimal choice to maximize winning chances as the game develops.

Final Answer: 3
